Albuquerque by the numbers

Where is Albuquerque, and why does the setting matter to a seller?

Albuquerque is the most populous city in New Mexico and the county seat of Bernalillo County. It sits in the Albuquerque Basin, with the Sandia Mountains to the east, the West Mesa to the west and the Rio Grande running north to south through the middle.

According to Wikipedia's Albuquerque entry, the city was founded in 1706 as La Villa de Alburquerque, counted 564,559 residents in the 2020 census, and covers about 189.5 square miles. Elevation runs from roughly 4,900 feet near the river to more than 6,700 feet in the foothills of Sandia Heights. A house in the valley and one in the foothills can differ in age, lot type and exposure to weather even when they share a ZIP code area.

For a seller, the practical point is that the tax bill follows the parcel, not the neighborhood name. Two houses a few blocks apart can sit in different taxing districts or inside a special improvement district, and the amounts on the bill reflect that.

Who actually bills property tax in Albuquerque?

The Bernalillo County Treasurer bills and collects property tax for Albuquerque addresses, and the Bernalillo County Assessor sets the value. The city does not mail a separate property tax bill.

The Assessor's frequently asked questions page lays out the yearly sequence. The Assessor delivers the tax roll to the Treasurer by October 1, and the state Department of Finance and Administration sets rates county by county in September. The Treasurer then mails bills. For 2026, the county said bills would go out by November 2 because November 1 fell on a Sunday.

The Treasurer's office is at 415 Silver Ave SW in downtown Albuquerque and can be reached at (505) 468-7031. The same building houses the Assessor at (505) 222-3700.

What are the Albuquerque property tax dates?

First-half tax is due November 10 and second-half tax is due April 10, with late fees starting December 10 and May 10 respectively. The table below sets out the calendar as the county publishes it.

DateWhat happensSource
January 1Property is valued as it stands, assessed to the owner of recordBernalillo County Assessor FAQ
April 1Notices of Value must be mailedBernalillo County Assessor FAQ
30 days after mailingValuation protest and exemption applications dueBernalillo County Assessor
October 1Assessor delivers the tax roll to the TreasurerBernalillo County Assessor FAQ
November 1Bills mailed and available onlineBernalillo County Treasurer
November 10First half dueBernalillo County Treasurer
December 10Late fees begin on the first halfBernalillo County Treasurer
April 10Second half dueBernalillo County Treasurer
May 10Late fees begin on the second halfBernalillo County Treasurer

The county's important dates page is the one to check before you rely on any date, since the calendar can shift when a deadline lands on a weekend.

What happens if Albuquerque property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid tax collects interest of 1% per month plus a penalty of 1% per month, with the penalty capped at 5% and a minimum of $5. Those are the figures on the Treasurer's FAQ page.

The county also says owners remain liable even if no bill arrives. In January 2026 it reported that roughly 10,600 bills had come back undelivered after the November mailing, mostly because of outdated mailing addresses, and it reminded owners to keep Notice of Value and bill addresses current. A seller who has moved out of an inherited or rented house is the most likely person to miss a bill.

In June the Treasurer mails delinquent notices. In its June 2026 update the office said it had collected about $917.5 million in property taxes that year, a collection rate of nearly 95%, which means a meaningful share of accounts still carry a balance after the second half falls due.

Owners who cannot pay in full are encouraged to call the Treasurer to set up payment arrangements. A monthly payment option also exists.

Can an Albuquerque homeowner protest the value or lower the bill?

Yes. A valuation protest goes to the Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing, and several tax savings programs have the same 30-day window.

The Assessor's protest page describes online filing through its appeal portal or in person at 415 Silver Ave SW. After a protest, an informal meeting with a field appraiser comes first, then a hearing before the Protest Valuation Review Board if the value is not settled. Owners who miss the window can still pay the bill and file a claim for refund in the Second Judicial District Court at 400 Lomas Blvd NW, where the county lists a $132 filing fee.

Programs the Assessor lists include:

  • Head of Family, which cuts taxable value by $2,000 and applies to one property in the state per household.
  • The veteran exemption, worth up to $10,000 off taxable value, with a state Veterans' Service Commission certificate.
  • A value freeze for owners 65 or older with modified gross income of $42,900 or less, or disabled owners at $41,900 or less, which holds the assessed value but not the tax rate.

The Assessor also states plainly that New Mexico has no homestead exemption. Taxable value is one-third of assessed value, and the Head of Family and veteran amounts come off that taxable figure.

What are public improvement districts, and do they affect an Albuquerque sale?

A public improvement district, or PID, is an extra charge on the tax bill that repays bonds used to build neighborhood infrastructure. Some Albuquerque subdivisions sit inside one.

The Assessor's FAQ explains that the amount per parcel changes from year to year, that parcel size and other factors affect it, and that a buyer continues the remaining bond payments where the seller left off. It also says an owner may pay a PID off early, and that the only exemption on PID payments is the 100% disabled veteran waiver.

If your house is in one, tell your buyer or your title company early. A cash buyer will price the remaining balance in, and a seller who knows the payoff figure avoids a late surprise at closing. The county Assessor keeps a page listing the name and boundary of each district.

Do Albuquerque's short-term rental rules matter if I want to sell?

They matter if the house has been rented by the night, because the city requires a permit and enforces it. A short-term rental in Albuquerque is a dwelling or part of one rented for stays under 29 consecutive days.

According to the city's Planning Department FAQ, the permit needs a business license, a floor plan, proof of insurance of at least $250,000 per unit, and a posted Good Neighbor Agreement. The fee is $120 in the first year and $90 for renewals. Operators must also file a monthly lodgers' tax report by the 25th, even when a platform remits the tax. Running a rental without a permit can bring fines and a bar on future operation.

A seller with an unpermitted rental history has a reason to sort that out before listing or accepting an offer.

What do Albuquerque sellers commonly run into?

Most delays come from paperwork, not from the market. Typical issues are listed below.

  • A tax bill that went to an old address and is now delinquent.
  • A PID balance that was not known until the title search.
  • An unpermitted short-term rental or an unfinished addition that changes the assessed value.
  • A deed that never moved into an heir's name after a death.

The city's main employers add some context. Wikipedia's list of Albuquerque's largest employers starts with Kirtland Air Force Base, the University of New Mexico and Sandia National Laboratories, followed by Albuquerque Public Schools and Presbyterian Healthcare Services.

Whichever way you sell, the unpaid tax comes out of the proceeds at closing through the title company, and the first thing to do is pull the balance from the Treasurer's online tax search.

More questions about Albuquerque, NM Property Tax Guide

Does the City of Albuquerque send its own property tax bill?

No. Bernalillo County bills Albuquerque property owners. The Assessor sets the value, the Treasurer mails the bill and collects, and the state sets the rates each September.

When is Albuquerque property tax due?

Half is due November 10 and half is due April 10. Late fees begin December 10 on the first half and May 10 on the second half, according to the Bernalillo County Treasurer.

How much are the late fees on Albuquerque property tax?

Interest is 1% of the unpaid tax each month, and the penalty is 1% each month up to 5%, with a $5 minimum penalty. The Treasurer lists these on its FAQ page.

Can I sell my Albuquerque house if I still owe property tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax, with any penalty and interest, is normally paid from the sale proceeds by the title company at closing. Check the exact balance with the Bernalillo County Treasurer first.

Is there a homestead exemption in Albuquerque?

No. New Mexico has no homestead exemption. The Assessor offers Head of Family, which reduces taxable value by $2,000, plus veteran exemptions and a value freeze for qualifying owners.

Do I need a permit to rent my Albuquerque home by the night?

Yes. Albuquerque requires a short-term rental permit and a business license before you advertise stays under 29 days. The permit fee is $120 the first year and $90 on renewal.

Santa Fe by the numbers

Where is Santa Fe and who sends the property tax bill?

Santa Fe sits in the Northern Rio Grande Valley at the southern end of the Sangre de Cristo mountains, at about 7,000 feet above sea level. The US EPA describes it as the highest and oldest state capital in the United States, founded in the early 1600s. The Library of Congress state guide dates its start as capital to 1610.

The bill itself does not come from City Hall. In New Mexico the county runs the process, so a Santa Fe homeowner deals with two county offices: the Assessor, who sets the value, and the Treasurer, who mails the bill and collects the money. Both are part of Santa Fe County government.

QuestionOfficeWhat the office says
Who values my house?Santa Fe County AssessorMails a Notice of Value each year, typically on or around April 1
Who bills and collects?Santa Fe County TreasurerBills are mailed around the end of October or the start of November
Where do I pay?Treasurer, 100 Catron St.Online portal, phone, mail (P.O. Box T, Santa Fe, NM 87504) or in person
Who hears a value appeal?County Valuation Protest BoardThree members, one from the State Property Tax Division

When are Santa Fe property taxes due?

The Santa Fe County Treasurer's page lists upcoming deadlines of November 12 and December 10, with tax becoming delinquent on the 11th, and a second half due on or before May 10. The same page also carries an older line saying the first half is due on or before December 1, so the two do not match exactly.

Because of that mismatch, check the due date printed on your own bill before you plan a closing around it. The Treasurer's page is the place to confirm it.

What happens if a payment is late is stated clearly on that page:

  • Interest starts on the thirtieth day after the due date and runs at 1 percent a month, or any fraction of a month, which is 12 percent a year (Section 7-38-49 NMSA 1978).
  • A penalty of 1 percent of the delinquent tax applies for each month or part of a month, capped at 5 percent.
  • Where the penalty would come to under five dollars, it is five dollars.

The Treasurer also takes a monthly payment plan application, and bills can be viewed with ten years of tax history in the online portal. A card payment carries a 2.5 percent transaction fee and an e-check carries a flat $1.95, according to the office.

How does the Santa Fe County Assessor set my value?

The Assessor re-appraises property every year, and the value on a notice reflects the prior year's market value. A 2024 notice, for example, reflected 2023 market value, according to the Assessor's help guide.

Residential property has a limit. Under state law, the valuation of a house, apartment or manufactured home cannot rise more than 3 percent a year over the prior year's assessed value. The guide gives an example: a $100,000 value in 2022 could not exceed $103,000 in 2023 or $106,090 in 2024.

Taxable value is one third of the appraised value. The county's own example takes a $150,000 appraisal, divides by three to reach $50,000, and multiplies by a sample rate of 0.0270380 to get $1,351.19. The rate in that example is for illustration only, and we do not state a current Santa Fe rate because we could not confirm one on an opened page.

This matters to a seller in one specific way. The Assessor's guide notes that the 3 percent cap applies while the same owner holds the property. A change of ownership, including a transfer between an LLC and its members as decided by the New Mexico Court of Appeals in Giddings v. SRT Mountain Vista, LLC, ends the cap, and the property is then assessed at market value. A buyer of a long-held Santa Fe house can therefore receive a larger bill than the seller paid.

How do I protest a Santa Fe property value?

File a petition of protest with the County Assessor within 30 days of the official mailing date of the Notice of Value. The Assessor's pamphlet says notices typically go out on or around April 1, and that in some years the date moves. In 2024 the notice went out May 1 and the deadline moved with it.

The steps, as the Assessor describes them:

  1. An appraiser reviews the property on site, taking photos, checking the exterior and correcting data. The appraiser then writes to tell you whether the value changed.
  2. If you still disagree, you may be invited to an informal conference where you can bring comparable sales and other evidence.
  3. If that fails, a formal hearing is held before the County Valuation Protest Board, with notice by certified mail at least 15 days ahead. The board mails its written decision within 30 days of the hearing.

By law protests are to be resolved within 180 days of the filing date, though the State Property Tax Director can extend that. Bring five copies of any documents, and give a copy to the appraiser at least 30 days before the hearing. A protestant who does not appear loses by default. Protests can also be filed online through the Assessor's portal.

Which exemptions can lower a Santa Fe County tax bill?

Four are listed in the Assessor's help guide, and each has to be claimed within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing date.

  • Head of Family: a $2,000 reduction in taxable value of residential real estate. Only one person per household can claim it, and only in one county in the state.
  • Veteran: a $4,000 reduction for an honorably discharged veteran or an unmarried surviving spouse who holds a certificate of eligibility from the New Mexico Department of Veterans' Services. It stays on the property until ownership changes, and it must be claimed in person.
  • 100 percent disabled veteran: a full exemption on the residence, again lasting until ownership changes.
  • Valuation freeze: for owners 65 or older or permanently disabled with modified gross income of $41,900 or less in 2023 (the figure in the 2024 guide). Proof of income and age or disability is required.

Since several of these end when ownership changes, a buyer has to apply again. A seller does not need to do anything, but should know that a lowered bill will not follow the house to the next owner automatically.

What does the Santa Fe economy look like?

Government is the largest single block of jobs in the Santa Fe metro area. The Bureau of Labor Statistics shows total nonfarm employment at about 63,500 in September 2026 (preliminary), with government at roughly 15,000, education and health services near 11,800, and leisure and hospitality near 11,400.

The same release puts the unemployment rate at 4.3 percent in September 2026 (preliminary), after 4.9 percent in July. Those are metro-area figures, not city-only, and BLS labels the latest month as preliminary.

The EPA notes that tourism draws on the city's cultural significance and outdoor recreation. About 37 percent of Santa Fe households rent, according to the Census Bureau figures already shown on this page.

Do Santa Fe's historic districts and short-term rental rules affect a sale?

They can. Santa Fe has several historic districts, among them the Don Gaspar Area, Westside-Guadalupe, Historic Transition and Historic Review districts, and exterior alterations in them go through the city's Historic Preservation Division and the Historic Districts Review Board. The city's preservation report describes historic status review as an added step for exterior work.

If you plan repairs before selling, such as new windows, stucco or a roofline change, ask the Historic Preservation Division (505-955-6605 appears on city agendas) whether the property is in a district first. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is avoids that step for the seller.

Short-term rentals are also regulated. The city says anyone who owns or operates a short-term rental in calendar year 2026 must hold an STR permit, plus a city business license. A seller who has been renting a house this way should check whether the permit is current, because it affects what a buyer can do with the property.

What should I do about tax due when I sell a Santa Fe house?

Get the payoff from the Treasurer, then let the closing agent pay it out of your proceeds. The title company reads the county record, deducts what is owed, and sends it to the Treasurer.

  • Pull the bill and ten-year history from the Treasurer's online portal.
  • Ask whether interest and penalty are running, using the 1 percent monthly rules above.
  • Check that any protest you filed is resolved or disclosed.
  • Tell your buyer if an exemption or valuation freeze will end at transfer.

If back tax is the reason you want to sell, a cash sale with no repairs can close on a schedule that fits the debt. We do not promise a price here, because the offer depends on the house.

More questions about Santa Fe, NM Property Tax Guide

When are Santa Fe property taxes due?

The Santa Fe County Treasurer's page lists November 12 and December 10 as upcoming deadlines, with tax delinquent on the 11th, and a second half due on or before May 10. The page also shows an older December 1 line, so confirm the date printed on your bill.

Does the City of Santa Fe collect property tax?

No. The Santa Fe County Assessor sets the value and the Santa Fe County Treasurer bills and collects it. Both offices are county offices.

How long do I have to protest my Santa Fe value?

You have 30 days from the official mailing date of the Notice of Value. The Assessor says notices typically go out on or around April 1, but the date can shift in a given year.

What is the penalty on late Santa Fe property tax?

Interest runs at 1 percent a month from the thirtieth day after the due date, and a penalty of 1 percent a month applies up to a cap of 5 percent, according to the Treasurer.

Does the 3 percent cap on increases follow the house to a buyer?

No. The Assessor's guide says a change of ownership ends the limit on a residential property, and the house is then assessed at market value.

Can I sell a Santa Fe house with property tax unpaid?

Yes. The closing agent pays the amount owed to the Treasurer from the sale proceeds. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer before closing.
